title: The Unexpected Playlist
premise: Lena Dunmore, the only out kid in the fading town of Harrow Creek, has survived high school by keeping her head down—until sorting her late grandmother's recipe box reveals index cards that aren't recipes at all, but coded instructions leading to a hidden cache of letters documenting a decades-old town secret: the flood of 1974 that drowned the old mill district wasn't an accident. As Lena deciphers the cards with the help of Theo, her estranged childhood best friend whose family helped cover it up, she realizes the 'price of survival' her grandmother paid was silence—and that staying invisible was never really an option. When the truth threatens to destroy Theo's family and reignite old wounds, Lena must choose between protecting the friendship and telling the truth, publishing her grandmother's letters even as the town's power brokers close ranks. In the end, the truth comes out at the centennial memorial, costing Lena almost everything except herself—and giving the drowned families' descendants, including Theo's own mother, their names back.
about_author: Freya Halloran grew up in a small river town where everyone knew everyone's business except the things that mattered. She writes stories about queer kids in quiet places who discover that silence is never as safe as it promises to be.

chapters.title: Fine
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Establishing chapter: Lena navigates another invisible week at Harrow Creek High, performing 'fine' for classmates, her grieving mother, and herself. The emotional beat is weary self-protection—the armor of a girl who learned early that being seen costs something.

chapters.title: The Recipe Box
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Clearing out Grandma Ada's kitchen, Lena finds the oak recipe box and, tucked beneath the cardamom bread, an index card reading 'Step one: tell no one until you've read them all.' Curiosity cracks her numbness; the beat is a first spark of intrigue.

chapters.title: Cards That Aren't for Food
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. At night she sorts forty cards written in Ada's cipher-like shorthand—directions to locations, dates, initials. One references 'the mill kids.' The beat is dawning unease: her grandmother was keeping something deliberate, not sentimental.

chapters.title: Theo
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Deciphering requires someone who knew Ada too—forcing Lena to approach Theo Marsh, her former best friend, estranged since middle school after Lena came out and his family pulled away. Awkward truce over the kitchen table; the beat is fragile, reluctant reconnection.

chapters.title: The Old Mill Road
chapters.summary: Alternating POV begins. Following card seven, Lena and Theo hike to the flooded mill district, now a weedy reservoir inlet. They find a rusted tin matching Ada's description. The beat is shared wonder tinged with dread—they're in this together whether they like it or not.

chapters.title: Letters Under Water Stain
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. The tin holds letters from 1973–74: Ada, then seventeen, writing to a friend about strange deliveries to the mill at night. The beat is intimacy across time—Lena meeting her grandmother as a girl, not a legend.

chapters.title: What the Town Remembers
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo researches the official story: the 1974 flood was natural, eleven dead, case closed. But his father goes pale when Theo mentions the mill. The beat is fear from the other side—we learn Theo has skin in the cover-up.

chapters.title: Card Nineteen
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. A card leads to Ada's old church pew, where a final letter names names: the mill owner diverted the levee to save his own property, drowning the workers' quarter—and Ada saw it happen. The beat is vertigo; the secret has faces.

chapters.title: Survival Is a Price
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Flashback-tinged chapter: Ada's last letter explains why she stayed silent—her family needed work, and speaking meant ruin. Lena recognizes her own strategy of invisibility mirrored back. The beat is painful identification.

chapters.title: Someone Else Is Looking
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo's father confronts him: does he have Ada's papers? Someone ransacked the Dunmore porch overnight. The beat is escalation—the past isn't passive; people still have stakes in the lie.

chapters.title: Split
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Theo begs Lena to stop before his family is destroyed; Lena refuses—Ada spent fifty years paying for silence and so has she. They part angry. The beat is heartbreak: truth versus loyalty made flesh.

chapters.title: The Centennial Committee
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Lena petitions the town council to include the letters in the upcoming centennial exhibit and is politely stonewalled by descendants of the mill owner. The beat is institutional stonewalling—invisibility enforced from above.

chapters.title: Mother Knows Something
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Lena finally shows her mother the letters; Mom confesses Ada told her fragments years ago and begged her never to look. Mother and daughter grieve together. The beat is unexpected alliance—family choosing truth over inherited fear.

chapters.title: Theo's Choice
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo finds his grandfather's name in Ada's letters—not as villain but as the young deputy ordered to look away. He understands complicity is inherited too. The beat is moral awakening through personal cost.

chapters.title: Break-In
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. The recipe box is stolen from her bedroom; only the cards remain hidden in her backpack. Terrified but galvanized, Lena photographs every letter and uploads them. The beat is defiance born of violation.

chapters.title: Deadline
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The centennial is Saturday. Council president Voss offers Lena a deal: donate the letters 'for safekeeping' and get a college recommendation letter. She recognizes hush money wearing a bow tie. The beat is temptation refused.

chapters.title: Reconciliation at the Reservoir
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo finds Lena at the water and gives her something he found in his grandfather's attic: photos proving the levee was cut. He's in, fully, whatever it costs. The beat is repaired trust, stronger for having broken.

chapters.title: Eleven Names
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Lena and Theo track down descendants of the flood victims, including Ruth Okafor, whose grandmother died at nineteen. Reading Ada's letters aloud, they turn victims back into people. The beat is communal grief becoming communal purpose.

chapters.title: The Night Before
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Quiet chapter: Lena prepares her speech, terrified of losing Theo again, her standing in town, her mother's safety. She rereads Ada's line: 'The price of survival is only worth paying once.' The beat is dread laced with resolve.

chapters.title: Centennial
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. At the ceremony, as Voss unveils a sanitized mural, Lena takes the stage and reads the eleven names and the truth. The room fractures—outrage, tears, denial—but Ruth stands beside her, then others. The beat is the climax: truth spoken publicly, irreversibly.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Consequences land: vandalism on the Dunmore porch, cold shoulders, but also a state investigation reopened and the reservoir slated for a memorial. Some friendships die; some, unexpectedly, deepen. The beat is costly, imperfect vindication.

chapters.title: Visible
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Epilogue in spring: Lena places the recipe box in the new memorial display, one card left blank—Ada's gift of an unwritten future. Theo walks beside her in daylight, unhidden. Final beat: Lena is fine, and for the first time, it isn't a performance.
